hook_text: Biodegradable is printed on a million packets. Here is how to tell when it actually means something.
clip_script: A banana peel disappears in weeks. A plastic bottle lasts five hundred years. The difference is one word: biodegradable. It means living things, bacteria and fungi, can eat the material and turn it into water, carbon dioxide and compost. Paper, cotton, wood, sugar-cane fibre: yes. Polythene, polystyrene, PVC: no, nothing on Earth can digest them, so they just crumble into microplastic. Now the catch. The word on the label only counts if you know three things. How long: months, not decades. Where: a home compost heap, or only a special factory you will never see. What is left: compost, or plastic dust. Then go bigger. Where did the material come from? How was it made? How long will you use it? What happens at the end? Ask those four questions of any two materials and count the wins. That is how a technologist tells green from greenwash.
visual_style: A banana peel fades to compost while a bottle beside it stays, then fragments into dots; a label with the word biodegradable gets three question marks; four life-cycle icons line up and tally.
pacing: Peel versus bottle, the definition, the three catches, the four questions.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run a takeaway container through the four life-cycle questions.
